decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Physiology of RBCs

cards.front: Why are RBCs biconcave?
cards.back: To increase membrane surface area for efficient gas exchange.

cards.front: Why must the RBC membrane be flexible?
cards.back: So RBCs can deform and pass through narrow capillaries without rupturing.

cards.front: What is the normal RBC lifespan?
cards.back: About 120 days (±7 days).

cards.front: How is most CO₂ transported in blood?
cards.back: About 70% as bicarbonate; ~20% binds hemoglobin as carbamino-Hb.

cards.front: Why is carbonic anhydrase important in RBCs?
cards.back: It rapidly supports CO₂ conversion to bicarbonate for CO₂ transport.

cards.front: Why is G6PD important in RBCs?
cards.back: It generates NADPH via the HMP shunt, helping maintain normal RBC fragility.

cards.front: What is the main physiological trigger for erythropoiesis?
cards.back: Tissue hypoxia.

cards.front: How does hypoxia increase RBC production?
cards.back: Hypoxia → ↑EPO → stimulation of erythropoiesis in bone marrow.

cards.front: Where is most erythropoietin produced?
cards.back: Kidney ~90%; liver ~10%.

cards.front: Where does adult erythropoiesis mainly occur?
cards.back: Red marrow of flat bones plus proximal parts of long bones.

cards.front: What supplies globin vs heme synthesis?
cards.back: High-value protein supplies globin; iron is required for heme.

cards.front: Why are vitamin B12 and folate needed for RBC production?
cards.back: They are required for normal maturation of RBC precursors.

cards.front: What happens to old RBCs after ~120 days?
cards.back: Macrophages—especially in spleen/lymphoid tissue—break them into heme and globin.

cards.front: What happens to heme after RBC breakdown?
cards.back: Heme → iron + biliverdin; biliverdin → bilirubin for biliary excretion.

cards.front: What does hematocrit measure?
cards.back: The percentage of whole-blood volume occupied by RBCs.

cards.front: What lowers vs raises hematocrit?
cards.back: Anemia/overhydration/pregnancy lower it; polycythemia/dehydration raise it.

cards.front: What causes RBC sedimentation in ESR?
cards.back: Rouleaux formation.

cards.front: Is ESR diagnostic of a specific disease?
cards.back: No. It is nonspecific and mainly useful as a prognostic/follow-up test.

decks.subject: Biochemistry
decks.title: Heme Synthesis

cards.front: What is heme structurally?
cards.back: An iron-containing porphyrin made of four pyrrole rings linked by methenyl bridges.

cards.front: Which organs are major sites of heme synthesis?
cards.back: Liver and erythroid bone marrow.

cards.front: Where do the steps of heme synthesis occur?
cards.back: First step + last 3 steps in mitochondria; intermediate steps in cytosol.

cards.front: What is the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis?
cards.back: ALA synthase forming δ-ALA from glycine + succinyl-CoA.

cards.front: Which cofactor does ALA synthase require?
cards.back: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).

cards.front: What converts ALA to porphobilinogen?
cards.back: ALA dehydratase (PBG synthase); it is inhibited by lead.

cards.front: What is the first pyrrole-containing intermediate?
cards.back: Porphobilinogen (PBG).

cards.front: What does PBG deaminase make?
cards.back: Four PBG molecules → hydroxymethylbilane.

cards.front: What happens without uroporphyrinogen III synthase?
cards.back: Hydroxymethylbilane converts nonenzymatically to uroporphyrinogen I.

cards.front: Which heme-synthesis enzymes are inhibited by lead?
cards.back: ALA dehydratase, coproporphyrinogen oxidase, and ferrochelatase.

cards.front: What does ferrochelatase do?
cards.back: Inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to form heme.

cards.front: How does heme regulate its own synthesis in liver?
cards.back: Heme/hemin inhibits hepatic ALA synthase.

cards.front: Why can phenobarbital or griseofulvin increase ALA synthase?
cards.back: They induce CYP450, consume heme, lower hepatic heme, and release ALA synthase from inhibition.

cards.front: Why do early-pathway porphyrias cause neurovisceral symptoms?
cards.back: ALA and PBG accumulate; they are neurotoxic.

cards.front: Why do later-pathway porphyrias cause photosensitivity?
cards.back: Porphyrins accumulate, absorb light, form free radicals, and damage skin.

cards.front: Best test during an acute porphyria attack?
cards.back: Urinary PBG measurement.

cards.front: How does IV hemin help acute porphyria?
cards.back: It suppresses ALA synthase activity.

cards.front: Preferred test for lead poisoning?
cards.back: Blood lead level because lead concentrates in erythrocytes.

decks.subject: Biochemistry
decks.title: Plasma Lipoprotein Metabolism

cards.front: What is in a lipoprotein core vs shell?
cards.back: Core: TAG + cholesteryl esters. Shell: apoproteins + phospholipids + free cholesterol.

cards.front: How do size and density change from CM to HDL?
cards.back: Size decreases while density increases: CM → VLDL → IDL → LDL → HDL.

cards.front: Main job of chylomicrons?
cards.back: Deliver dietary TAG to tissues and dietary cholesterol to the liver.

cards.front: Which apoprotein is unique to nascent chylomicrons?
cards.back: ApoB-48.

cards.front: What do nascent chylomicrons acquire from HDL?
cards.back: ApoC-II and ApoE.

cards.front: What activates lipoprotein lipase?
cards.back: ApoC-II; LPL is also stimulated by insulin.

cards.front: What does LPL do to chylomicrons/VLDL?
cards.back: Hydrolyzes their TAG to fatty acids and glycerol.

cards.front: How are chylomicron remnants cleared?
cards.back: Liver receptors recognize ApoE and internalize remnants by endocytosis.

cards.front: Main job of VLDL?
cards.back: Carry endogenous TAG from liver to extrahepatic tissues.

cards.front: What is the VLDL → LDL sequence?
cards.back: VLDL loses TAG → IDL → further delipidation → LDL.

cards.front: What is the only apoprotein on LDL?
cards.back: ApoB-100.

cards.front: What does the LDL receptor recognize?
cards.back: ApoB-100 and ApoE.

cards.front: What happens to excess intracellular cholesterol?
cards.back: ACAT re-esterifies it for intracellular storage.

cards.front: Two key roles of HDL in lipoprotein metabolism?
cards.back: Reservoir of ApoC-II/ApoE and mediator of reverse cholesterol transport.

cards.front: What activates LCAT?
cards.back: ApoA-I on nascent HDL.

cards.front: What does LCAT do?
cards.back: Esterifies free cholesterol on HDL, promoting HDL maturation.

cards.front: How does HDL mature?
cards.back: Nascent discoid HDL accumulates cholesteryl ester → HDL3 → HDL2.

cards.front: What does CETP exchange?
cards.back: Cholesteryl esters and triglycerides between HDL and TAG-rich lipoproteins.

decks.subject: Biochemistry
decks.title: Disorders of Plasma Lipoproteins

cards.front: Primary vs secondary hyperlipoproteinemia?
cards.back: Primary is inherited; secondary results from another disease, condition, or drug.

cards.front: Hypercholesterolemia classically presents with what major risk?
cards.back: Coronary heart disease via atherosclerosis.

cards.front: Severe hypertriglyceridemia can present with what acute complication?
cards.back: Acute pancreatitis.

cards.front: Common secondary causes of hyperlipoproteinemia?
cards.back: DM, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, CKD, obesity, alcohol, obstructive liver disease, drugs.

cards.front: How do trans fats affect LDL and HDL?
cards.back: Increase LDL and decrease HDL.

cards.front: Fredrickson type I: what is elevated?
cards.back: Chylomicrons → very high triglycerides; creamy top layer.

cards.front: Fredrickson type IIa: what is elevated?
cards.back: LDL → high cholesterol; serum remains clear.

cards.front: Fredrickson type IIb: what is elevated?
cards.back: LDL + VLDL → high cholesterol + triglycerides.

cards.front: Fredrickson type III: what is elevated?
cards.back: IDL → high cholesterol + triglycerides; dysbetalipoproteinemia.

cards.front: Fredrickson type IV: what is elevated?
cards.back: VLDL → high triglycerides.

cards.front: Fredrickson type V: what is elevated?
cards.back: VLDL + chylomicrons → very high TG + increased cholesterol.

cards.front: Cause of familial hyperchylomicronemia (type I)?
cards.back: LPL deficiency or ApoC-II deficiency.

cards.front: Major defects causing familial hypercholesterolemia?
cards.back: LDL receptor loss-of-function, ApoB loss-of-function, or PCSK9 gain-of-function.

cards.front: Why can Lp(a) promote thrombosis?
cards.back: Apo(a) resembles plasminogen and can inhibit fibrinolysis.

cards.front: What lipid pattern is strongly atherogenic?
cards.back: High LDL, low HDL, and hypertriglyceridemia.

cards.front: When should LDL be measured directly rather than Friedewald-calculated?
cards.back: When triglycerides are ≥400 mg/dL.

cards.front: What is non-HDL cholesterol?
cards.back: Total cholesterol − HDL cholesterol.

cards.front: What is remnant cholesterol?
cards.back: Total cholesterol − HDL − LDL.

cards.front: Core defect in abetalipoproteinemia?
cards.back: Impaired assembly of VLDL and chylomicrons → absent LDL/ApoB and fat malabsorption.

cards.front: Why is vitamin E deficiency dangerous in abetalipoproteinemia?
cards.back: It can cause progressive neurologic degeneration.

cards.front: What characterizes Tangier disease?
cards.back: Very low dysfunctional ApoA-I and markedly low HDL; orange tonsils and neuropathy may occur.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Heart as a Pump

cards.front: What mainly controls cardiac myocyte contraction strength?
cards.back: Extracellular Ca²⁺ influx; more Ca²⁺ has a positive inotropic effect.

cards.front: Why do Ca²⁺ channel blockers reduce cardiac contractility?
cards.back: They reduce Ca²⁺ influx needed for excitation–contraction coupling.

cards.front: What is preload in the intact heart?
cards.back: The resting initial fiber length, approximated by end-diastolic volume (EDV).

cards.front: State the Frank–Starling law.
cards.back: Within limits, greater initial cardiac muscle length → greater force of contraction.

cards.front: How does sympathetic venoconstriction affect preload?
cards.back: It increases venous return → increases EDV/preload.

cards.front: Major factors that increase venous return?
cards.back: Muscle pump, respiratory pump, cardiac suction, sympathetic venoconstriction, blood volume, stretchability.

cards.front: What is heterometric autoregulation?
cards.back: Increased contractile force caused by increased EDV (Frank–Starling mechanism).

cards.front: What is homeometric autoregulation?
cards.back: Increased contractile force secondary to increased aortic pressure without relying on increased fiber length.

cards.front: Why does Frank–Starling help equalize RV and LV output?
cards.back: More output from one side increases venous return/preload to the other side, raising its stroke volume.

cards.front: How does exercise raise cardiac output through preload?
cards.back: Muscle pump + sympathetic venoconstriction increase venous return and EDV → ↑SV.

cards.front: What is afterload in this lecture?
cards.back: Mean aortic pressure.

cards.front: How do SNS and epinephrine increase contractility?
cards.back: They increase Ca²⁺ influx and cross-bridge cycling at a given EDV.

cards.front: At the same EDV, what shows increased contractility?
cards.back: Lower ESV and therefore higher stroke volume.

cards.front: Typical example from the lecture: EDV 135 mL, ESV 65 mL gives what SV?
cards.back: 70 mL.

cards.front: With sympathetic stimulation: EDV 135 mL, ESV 35 mL gives what SV?

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What mainly controls long-term arterial pressure?
cards.back: Renal control of body fluid volume and sodium balance.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How does increased arterial pressure affect the kidneys?
cards.back: It increases pressure diuresis and pressure natriuresis, lowering blood volume and pressure.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What is pressure natriuresis?
cards.back: Increased renal sodium excretion caused by a rise in arterial pressure.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What is pressure diuresis?
cards.back: Increased renal water excretion caused by a rise in arterial pressure.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How does the renin-angiotensin system raise arterial pressure?
cards.back: Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and promotes renal sodium/water retention.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What triggers renin release?
cards.back: Reduced renal perfusion, low NaCl delivery to macula densa, and β1 sympathetic stimulation.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What does angiotensin II do to aldosterone?
cards.back: It stimulates aldosterone secretion, increasing distal sodium reabsorption.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How does aldosterone raise blood pressure?
cards.back: It increases renal sodium retention; water follows, increasing extracellular fluid and blood volume.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What is the role of ADH in blood-pressure regulation?
cards.back: It increases water reabsorption and, at high levels, can cause vasoconstriction.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What is the thirst mechanism's effect on blood pressure?
cards.back: It increases water intake, helping restore extracellular fluid and blood volume.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How does ANP oppose volume expansion?
cards.back: It promotes natriuresis and diuresis and inhibits renin/aldosterone effects.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: Why are kidneys essential in chronic hypertension?
cards.back: Sustained hypertension requires a renal-fluid balance shift that permits pressure to remain elevated.
tags: Intermediate and Long-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: Where are the main arterial baroreceptors?
cards.back: Carotid sinus and aortic arch.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What is systolic pressure?
cards.back: The maximum arterial pressure during ventricular systole; about 120 mmHg in the lecture example.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What is diastolic pressure?
cards.back: The minimum arterial pressure during ventricular diastole; about 80 mmHg in the lecture example.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How is pulse pressure calculated?
cards.back: Pulse pressure = systolic pressure − diastolic pressure.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How is mean arterial pressure approximated at normal heart rates?
cards.back: MAP ≈ diastolic pressure + 1/3 of pulse pressure.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What is the main relationship determining mean ABP?
cards.back: Mean ABP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What does stimulation of the pressor area do?
cards.back: Increases sympathetic and decreases vagal activity → tachycardia, increased contractility, vasoconstriction, increased CO and ABP.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What does stimulation of the depressor/cardioinhibitory area do?
cards.back: Increases vagal and decreases sympathetic activity → lower HR, lower contractility/CO, vasodilatation and lower ABP.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: Why does sympathetic tone to arterioles matter at rest?
cards.back: It helps maintain normal peripheral resistance and diastolic blood pressure.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: Why does sympathetic tone to veins matter?
cards.back: Venoconstriction increases venous return, preload, stroke volume and cardiac output.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What happens to baroreceptor firing when ABP rises?
cards.back: Arterial stretch increases baroreceptor firing to the medulla.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How does the baroreflex correct high ABP?
cards.back: ↑ baroreceptor firing → ↑ depressor/vagal and ↓ pressor/sympathetic activity → ↓ HR, contractility and vascular tone.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How does the baroreflex correct a sudden fall in ABP?
cards.back: Reduced baroreceptor firing → increased sympathetic/pressor activity → tachycardia, increased contractility and vasoconstriction.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: Which nerve carries carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents?
cards.back: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: Which nerve carries aortic arch baroreceptor afferents?
cards.back: Vagus nerve (CN X).
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: Why are baroreceptors mainly short-term regulators?
cards.back: They reset during sustained/chronic pressure changes.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: When does the peripheral chemoreceptor reflex become especially important?
cards.back: When mean ABP falls below about 60 mmHg.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors in marked hypotension?
cards.back: Low PO₂, high PCO₂ and increased H⁺.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: Where are peripheral chemoreceptors located?
cards.back: Carotid bodies and aortic bodies.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: What are the three major sources of peripheral resistance?
cards.back: Vessel diameter, blood viscosity, and vessel length; arteriolar diameter is the main variable determinant within one person.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: How does cold weather affect ABP in the lecture?
cards.back: Cold causes cutaneous vasoconstriction, increasing peripheral resistance and ABP.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

cards.front: At rest, which autonomic tone predominates at the heart?
cards.back: Vagal tone predominates over sympathetic tone.
tags: Short-Term Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: What are the two major circulations?
cards.back: Systemic and pulmonary circulation.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: Which side of the heart pumps into systemic circulation?
cards.back: The left ventricle.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: Which side of the heart pumps into pulmonary circulation?
cards.back: The right ventricle.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: Why is pulmonary arterial pressure lower than systemic arterial pressure?
cards.back: Pulmonary vascular resistance is much lower.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: What is cardiac output?
cards.back: Heart rate × stroke volume.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: What is stroke volume?
cards.back: End-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: What is ejection fraction?
cards.back: Stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume × 100%.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: What is mean arterial pressure approximately equal to?
cards.back: Cardiac output × total peripheral resistance.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: Where is most blood volume stored at rest?
cards.back: Systemic veins and venules; they act as capacitance vessels.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: Which vessels are the main resistance vessels?
cards.back: Arterioles.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: Why is blood velocity lowest in capillaries?
cards.back: Capillaries have the greatest total cross-sectional area.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

cards.front: What is the main function of capillaries?
cards.back: Exchange of gases, nutrients, fluid, and wastes between blood and tissues.
tags: Physiological Organization of the Cardiovascular System

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Coronary Circulation

cards.front: When does most left coronary blood flow occur?
cards.back: During diastole.

cards.front: Why is left coronary flow reduced during systole?
cards.back: Contracting myocardium compresses intramyocardial vessels.

cards.front: What is the main local regulator of coronary blood flow?
cards.back: Myocardial metabolic demand, especially local vasodilator metabolites such as adenosine.

cards.front: How much oxygen does the myocardium normally extract from coronary blood?
cards.back: A high fraction at rest, so increased demand is met mainly by increasing coronary flow.

cards.front: What strongly increases coronary blood flow during exercise?
cards.back: Increased myocardial metabolism and local vasodilation.

cards.front: What does coronary perfusion pressure mainly depend on?
cards.back: Aortic diastolic pressure minus ventricular pressure.

cards.front: Why can tachycardia reduce coronary perfusion?
cards.back: It shortens diastole, the main period of left coronary flow.

cards.front: Which coronary artery commonly supplies the AV node in right-dominant circulation?
cards.back: Right coronary artery.

cards.front: What is coronary flow reserve?
cards.back: The ability of coronary circulation to increase flow above resting levels.

cards.front: What causes functional hyperemia in the heart?
cards.back: Increased cardiac work raises metabolites, producing coronary vasodilation.

cards.front: Why is subendocardium especially vulnerable to ischemia?
cards.back: It experiences greatest systolic compression and high oxygen demand.

cards.front: What is autoregulation of coronary flow?
cards.back: Maintenance of relatively stable flow across a range of perfusion pressures via local vascular adjustments.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Cardiac Excitability and Automaticity

cards.front: What gives SA nodal cells automaticity?
cards.back: Their membrane potential slowly depolarizes spontaneously during phase 4.

cards.front: What ion current contributes to pacemaker phase 4 depolarization?
cards.back: The funny current (If), with inward Na⁺ current, plus Ca²⁺ entry.

cards.front: What causes the upstroke of the SA-node action potential?
cards.back: Ca²⁺ influx through L-type calcium channels.

cards.front: What causes repolarization in SA nodal cells?
cards.back: K⁺ efflux.

cards.front: What causes phase 0 in ventricular myocytes?
cards.back: Rapid Na⁺ influx through fast sodium channels.

cards.front: What causes the plateau phase of ventricular action potential?
cards.back: Balance between L-type Ca²⁺ influx and K⁺ efflux.

cards.front: Why is the cardiac refractory period long?
cards.back: The plateau prolongs the action potential, preventing tetanic contraction.

cards.front: What is the normal dominant pacemaker?
cards.back: SA node, because it has the fastest spontaneous firing rate.

cards.front: What happens to SA-node firing with sympathetic stimulation?
cards.back: β1 stimulation steepens phase 4 depolarization, increasing heart rate.

cards.front: What happens to SA-node firing with vagal stimulation?
cards.back: ACh increases K⁺ conductance and reduces cAMP, slowing pacemaker depolarization.

cards.front: Why is AV nodal conduction slow?
cards.back: Small fibers and Ca²⁺-dependent depolarization create slow conduction.

cards.front: What is the physiological purpose of AV nodal delay?
cards.back: It allows atrial contraction to complete ventricular filling before ventricular systole.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Hemostasis Disorders and Anticoagulants

cards.front: What does PT mainly assess?
cards.back: Extrinsic and common coagulation pathways.

cards.front: Which factor is especially reflected by PT?
cards.back: Factor VII, plus common-pathway factors X, V, II, and fibrinogen.

cards.front: What does aPTT mainly assess?
cards.back: Intrinsic and common coagulation pathways.

cards.front: Which factors are assessed by aPTT but not PT?
cards.back: Factors XII, XI, IX, and VIII.

cards.front: What pattern is typical of hemophilia A?
cards.back: Prolonged aPTT with normal PT and normal platelet count.

cards.front: What is hemophilia A caused by?
cards.back: Factor VIII deficiency.

cards.front: What is hemophilia B caused by?
cards.back: Factor IX deficiency.

cards.front: What is the typical lab pattern in vitamin K deficiency?
cards.back: PT rises first because factor VII has the shortest half-life.

cards.front: What is DIC?
cards.back: Systemic coagulation activation causing microthrombi, consumption of platelets/factors, and bleeding.

cards.front: What happens to fibrinogen and D-dimer in DIC?
cards.back: Fibrinogen decreases; D-dimer increases.

cards.front: How does heparin produce anticoagulation?
cards.back: It potentiates antithrombin, especially inhibiting thrombin and factor Xa.

cards.front: How does warfarin produce anticoagulation?
cards.back: It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Physiology of White Blood Cells

cards.front: Most abundant peripheral WBC?
cards.back: Neutrophils, about 60–70%.

cards.front: Main neutrophil function?
cards.back: Phagocytosis and first-line defense against bacteria.

cards.front: Main eosinophil associations?
cards.back: Parasitic infestation and allergy.

cards.front: Basophil mediators?
cards.back: Histamine, heparin, bradykinin, and serotonin.

cards.front: Monocytes become what in tissues?
cards.back: Macrophages.

cards.front: Diapedesis?
cards.back: Leukocytes squeezing through capillary walls into tissues.

cards.front: Chemotaxis?
cards.back: Directed movement toward infection by chemical attractants.

cards.front: Opsonization?
cards.back: Coating targets with antibodies or complement to facilitate phagocytosis.

cards.front: Humoral immunity leukocyte?
cards.back: B lymphocytes.

cards.front: Cellular immunity leukocyte in this lecture?
cards.back: T lymphocytes.

cards.front: Leukocytosis threshold?
cards.back: Above 11,000 WBC/mm³.

cards.front: Pyogenic infection pattern?
cards.back: Neutrophilia.

cards.front: Normal total WBC count?
Largest and strongest phagocytic WBC?
cards.back: Monocyte.

cards.front: Parasitic infestation pattern?
cards.back: Eosinophilia.

cards.front: Allergic disease pattern?
cards.back: Basophilia.

cards.front: Tuberculosis pattern in this lecture?
cards.back: Lymphocytosis.

cards.front: Malaria pattern in this lecture?
cards.back: Monocytosis.

cards.front: Recruitment/phagocytosis sequence?
cards.back: Margination → diapedesis → chemotaxis → amoeboid movement → opsonization → phagocytosis.

cards.front: Leukopenia threshold?
cards.back: Below 4,000 WBC/mm³.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Hemostasis I

cards.front: What are the main stages of hemostasis?
cards.back: Vasoconstriction, platelet plug formation, coagulation, and clot stabilization/removal.

cards.front: What initiates platelet adhesion at damaged endothelium?
cards.back: Exposure of subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor.

cards.front: Which platelet receptor binds vWF?
cards.back: GPIb.

cards.front: Which platelet receptor mediates aggregation via fibrinogen?
cards.back: GPIIb/IIIa.

cards.front: What do activated platelets release to recruit more platelets?
cards.back: ADP and thromboxane A₂, among other mediators.

cards.front: What is the role of thromboxane A₂?
cards.back: Promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.

cards.front: What begins the extrinsic coagulation pathway?
cards.back: Tissue factor exposure activates factor VII.

cards.front: What is the key convergence point of coagulation pathways?
cards.back: Activation of factor X to Xa.

cards.front: What does factor Xa do in the prothrombinase complex?
cards.back: Converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa).

cards.front: What does thrombin do to fibrinogen?
cards.back: Converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

cards.front: What is the role of factor XIII?
cards.back: Cross-links fibrin, stabilizing the clot.

cards.front: How is fibrin removed after healing?
cards.back: Plasmin degrades fibrin during fibrinolysis.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Anemias and Polycythemia

cards.front: What is anemia physiologically?
cards.back: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, usually from low hemoglobin.

cards.front: How does anemia affect blood viscosity?
cards.back: It lowers viscosity.

cards.front: Why can cardiac output increase in anemia?
cards.back: Lower viscosity reduces resistance and tissue hypoxia promotes vasodilation and sympathetic compensation.

cards.front: What is microcytic anemia commonly associated with?
cards.back: Iron deficiency or impaired hemoglobin synthesis.

cards.front: What is macrocytic/megaloblastic anemia commonly associated with?
cards.back: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

cards.front: What is hemolytic anemia?
cards.back: Anemia due to premature destruction of RBCs.

cards.front: What is polycythemia?
cards.back: An abnormal increase in RBC mass/hematocrit.

cards.front: What is primary polycythemia?
cards.back: Polycythemia vera: autonomous marrow RBC production, usually with low EPO.

cards.front: What is secondary polycythemia?
cards.back: Increased RBC production driven by elevated EPO, commonly from hypoxia.

cards.front: How does polycythemia affect blood viscosity?
cards.back: It increases viscosity, which can slow blood flow and raise vascular resistance.

cards.front: Why does high altitude cause secondary polycythemia?
cards.back: Chronic hypoxemia stimulates renal EPO production.

cards.front: What happens to EPO in polycythemia vera vs hypoxic polycythemia?
cards.back: Low in polycythemia vera; high in hypoxia-driven secondary polycythemia.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Biochemistry
decks.title: Cholesterol Metabolism

cards.front: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis?
cards.back: HMG-CoA reductase.

cards.front: Where does cholesterol synthesis mainly occur?
cards.back: Especially liver; synthesis occurs in the cytosol and smooth ER.

cards.front: What does HMG-CoA reductase convert?
cards.back: HMG-CoA to mevalonate.

cards.front: How does high intracellular cholesterol affect HMG-CoA reductase?
cards.back: It suppresses cholesterol synthesis by downregulating the enzyme.

cards.front: How does insulin affect HMG-CoA reductase?
cards.back: It promotes the active dephosphorylated state and favors cholesterol synthesis.

cards.front: How does glucagon affect HMG-CoA reductase?
cards.back: It favors phosphorylation and inhibition of the enzyme.

cards.front: What drugs directly inhibit HMG-CoA reductase?
cards.back: Statins.

cards.front: What are major uses of cholesterol in the body?
cards.back: Membranes, steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D.

cards.front: What is the main route of cholesterol elimination?
cards.back: Conversion to bile acids and secretion of cholesterol/bile acids in bile.

cards.front: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis?
cards.back: Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase.

cards.front: How does LDL deliver cholesterol to cells?
cards.back: ApoB-100 binds LDL receptors, leading to receptor-mediated endocytosis.

cards.front: How does cellular cholesterol affect LDL receptors?
cards.back: High intracellular cholesterol reduces LDL-receptor expression.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Biochemistry
decks.title: Heme Catabolism and Bilirubin

cards.front: Where are senescent RBCs mainly removed?
cards.back: Reticuloendothelial macrophages, especially spleen, liver, and bone marrow.

cards.front: What enzyme opens the heme ring?
cards.back: Heme oxygenase.

cards.front: What is the first colored product of heme breakdown?
cards.back: Biliverdin.

cards.front: What converts biliverdin to bilirubin?
cards.back: Biliverdin reductase.

cards.front: How is unconjugated bilirubin transported in plasma?
cards.back: Bound to albumin.

cards.front: Why is unconjugated bilirubin not excreted in urine?
cards.back: It is water-insoluble and albumin-bound.

cards.front: What enzyme conjugates bilirubin in the liver?
cards.back: UDP-glucuronyl transferase.

cards.front: What happens to conjugated bilirubin after secretion into bile?
cards.back: Gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen.

cards.front: What gives stool its brown color?
cards.back: Stercobilin, derived from urobilinogen.

cards.front: What gives urine its yellow color?
cards.back: Urobilin, derived from urobilinogen.

cards.front: What pattern is typical of hemolysis?
cards.back: Predominantly increased unconjugated bilirubin.

cards.front: Why can conjugated bilirubin appear in urine?
cards.back: It is water-soluble and can be filtered when elevated in blood.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Biochemistry
decks.title: Plasma Proteins

cards.front: What is the most abundant plasma protein?
cards.back: Albumin.

cards.front: Where is albumin synthesized?
cards.back: Liver.

cards.front: What is albumin's major hemodynamic function?
cards.back: Maintains plasma colloid oncotic pressure.

cards.front: What happens to fluid balance when albumin falls markedly?
cards.back: Plasma oncotic pressure falls, favoring edema.

cards.front: What substances can albumin transport?
cards.back: Fatty acids, bilirubin, hormones, calcium, and many drugs.

cards.front: Which plasma protein fraction contains most antibodies?
cards.back: Gamma globulins.

cards.front: Where are immunoglobulins produced?
cards.back: Plasma cells, not hepatocytes.

cards.front: What is an acute-phase protein?
cards.back: A plasma protein whose concentration changes significantly during inflammation.

cards.front: Give a positive acute-phase protein example.
cards.back: C-reactive protein or fibrinogen.

cards.front: What happens to albumin during inflammation?
cards.back: It behaves as a negative acute-phase protein and may decrease.

cards.front: What is the main role of fibrinogen?
cards.back: It is converted to fibrin during coagulation.

cards.front: How can high fibrinogen affect ESR?
cards.back: It promotes rouleaux formation, increasing ESR.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Hematology
decks.title: Hemolytic Anemia

cards.front: What defines hemolytic anemia?
cards.back: Premature RBC destruction that exceeds marrow replacement.

cards.front: What marrow response is expected in hemolysis?
cards.back: Reticulocytosis, if marrow function and substrates are adequate.

cards.front: What happens to unconjugated bilirubin in hemolysis?
cards.back: It increases.

cards.front: What happens to LDH in hemolysis?
cards.back: It increases.

cards.front: What happens to haptoglobin in intravascular hemolysis?
cards.back: It decreases because it binds free hemoglobin.

cards.front: What is intravascular hemolysis?
cards.back: RBC destruction within the circulation, releasing hemoglobin into plasma.

cards.front: What is extravascular hemolysis?
cards.back: RBC removal by macrophages, mainly in spleen and liver.

cards.front: What is a key feature of hereditary spherocytosis?
cards.back: Spherocytes with membrane-cytoskeleton defects and splenic destruction.

cards.front: Why can G6PD deficiency cause episodic hemolysis?
cards.back: Oxidative stress cannot be adequately neutralized because NADPH generation is impaired.

cards.front: What is the mechanism of sickle-cell hemolysis?
cards.back: Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes, deforming RBCs and causing hemolysis/vaso-occlusion.

cards.front: What does a positive direct Coombs test suggest?
cards.back: Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia with antibody/complement bound to RBCs.

cards.front: What can chronic hemolysis cause in the gallbladder?
cards.back: Pigment gallstones due to increased bilirubin turnover.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pathology
decks.title: Vasculitis and Vascular & Cardiac Tumours

cards.front: What is vasculitis?
cards.back: Inflammation and damage of blood-vessel walls.

cards.front: How are vasculitides commonly classified?
cards.back: By the predominant size of vessel involved: large, medium, or small.

cards.front: What vessels are classically affected in giant-cell arteritis?
cards.back: Large and medium arteries, especially branches of the carotid artery.

cards.front: Why is giant-cell arteritis an emergency when vision symptoms occur?
cards.back: Ophthalmic artery involvement can cause irreversible blindness.

cards.front: What is Takayasu arteritis known for clinically?
cards.back: Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis causing weak/absent upper-extremity pulses.

cards.front: What is polyarteritis nodosa?
cards.back: Necrotizing vasculitis of medium/small muscular arteries, typically sparing pulmonary arteries.

cards.front: Which vasculitis is strongly associated with asthma and eosinophilia?
cards.back: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

cards.front: What is granulomatosis with polyangiitis characterized by?
cards.back: Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of respiratory tract plus small-vessel vasculitis and glomerulonephritis.

cards.front: What is a hemangioma?
cards.back: A benign vascular tumor composed of blood-filled vascular channels.

cards.front: What is angiosarcoma?
cards.back: A malignant endothelial vascular tumor.

cards.front: What is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults?
cards.back: Atrial myxoma.

cards.front: Where are cardiac myxomas commonly located?
cards.back: Usually in the left atrium, often attached near the fossa ovalis.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pathology
decks.title: Myocarditis and Pericardial Diseases

cards.front: What is myocarditis?
cards.back: Inflammation of myocardium with associated myocyte injury.

cards.front: What is a common cause of myocarditis?
cards.back: Viral infection is a common cause; immune-mediated and toxic causes also occur.

cards.front: What symptoms can myocarditis cause?
cards.back: Chest pain, arrhythmias, heart failure, or sudden cardiac death.

cards.front: What can severe myocarditis progress to?
cards.back: Dilated cardiomyopathy and chronic heart failure.

cards.front: What is pericarditis?
cards.back: Inflammation of the pericardial sac.

cards.front: What is the classic pain pattern in acute pericarditis?
cards.back: Sharp pleuritic pain improved by sitting up and leaning forward.

cards.front: What physical finding is classic in acute pericarditis?
cards.back: Pericardial friction rub.

cards.front: What is a pericardial effusion?
cards.back: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial cavity.

cards.front: What is cardiac tamponade?
cards.back: Hemodynamic compromise from pericardial pressure restricting cardiac filling.

cards.front: Why can rapidly accumulating pericardial fluid be dangerous even at modest volume?
cards.back: The stiff pericardium cannot stretch quickly, so pressure rises sharply.

cards.front: What is constrictive pericarditis?
cards.back: Fibrotic/calcified pericardium restricts diastolic ventricular filling.

cards.front: What is the key hemodynamic problem in tamponade?
cards.back: Impaired ventricular filling reduces stroke volume and cardiac output.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pathology
decks.title: Ischemic Heart Disease I

cards.front: What is ischemic heart disease?
cards.back: Myocardial dysfunction caused by an imbalance between coronary blood supply and oxygen demand.

cards.front: What is the most common underlying cause of IHD?
cards.back: Coronary atherosclerosis.

cards.front: What usually causes stable angina?
cards.back: Fixed atherosclerotic narrowing that limits flow during increased demand.

cards.front: What usually causes unstable angina?
cards.back: Plaque disruption with non-occlusive thrombosis and reduced coronary flow.

cards.front: What is myocardial infarction?
cards.back: Ischemic necrosis of myocardium from prolonged severe reduction in coronary blood flow.

cards.front: What most commonly triggers an acute MI?
cards.back: Rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed thrombosis.

cards.front: What is the main difference between angina and MI histologically?
cards.back: Angina causes reversible ischemia; MI causes irreversible myocyte necrosis.

cards.front: Why is subendocardial myocardium especially vulnerable to ischemia?
cards.back: It has high wall stress and the least favorable perfusion during systole.

cards.front: What is sudden cardiac death often caused by in IHD?
cards.back: A fatal ventricular arrhythmia triggered by ischemia.

cards.front: What is chronic ischemic heart disease?
cards.back: Progressive heart failure from repeated ischemic injury and myocardial loss.

cards.front: What determines infarct size?
cards.back: Site/severity of occlusion, duration, collateral flow, demand, and reperfusion.

cards.front: Why does early reperfusion matter in acute MI?
cards.back: It can salvage reversibly injured myocardium before necrosis becomes complete.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pathology
decks.title: Ischemic Heart Disease II

cards.front: When do irreversible myocyte injury and necrosis begin after severe ischemia?
cards.back: They begin after roughly 20–40 minutes of severe ischemia, then progress with time.

cards.front: What is the earliest major histologic pattern of MI necrosis?
cards.back: Coagulative necrosis.

cards.front: Which inflammatory cells dominate early after MI?
cards.back: Neutrophils.

cards.front: Which cells remove necrotic myocardium several days after MI?
cards.back: Macrophages.

cards.front: Why is the myocardium mechanically weakest several days after MI?
cards.back: Macrophages remove dead tissue before strong collagen scar has formed.

cards.front: What major complication can occur from papillary muscle rupture?
cards.back: Acute severe mitral regurgitation.

cards.front: What can free-wall rupture after MI cause?
cards.back: Hemopericardium and cardiac tamponade.

cards.front: What can interventricular septal rupture cause?
cards.back: An acute ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunt.

cards.front: What is a ventricular aneurysm after MI?
cards.back: A late scarred bulge of infarcted ventricular wall that can cause HF, arrhythmia, or mural thrombus.

cards.front: What is reperfusion injury?
cards.back: Additional injury after restored blood flow, involving oxidative stress, calcium overload, and inflammation.

cards.front: What is contraction-band necrosis associated with?
cards.back: Reperfusion and intense calcium influx into damaged myocytes.

cards.front: What eventually replaces a healed transmural MI?
cards.back: Dense collagenous scar.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pathology
decks.title: Lymphadenopathy

cards.front: What is lymphadenopathy?
cards.back: Abnormal enlargement or altered consistency of lymph nodes.

cards.front: What is reactive lymphadenitis?
cards.back: Benign lymph-node enlargement caused by immune response to infection or inflammation.

cards.front: What does follicular hyperplasia reflect?
cards.back: B-cell stimulation with enlarged reactive germinal centers.

cards.front: What does paracortical hyperplasia reflect?
cards.back: T-cell-zone expansion, often in viral infections or drug reactions.

cards.front: What is sinus histiocytosis?
cards.back: Expansion of lymph-node sinuses by macrophages, often draining cancer or inflammation.

cards.front: What features make a lymph node more suspicious for malignancy?
cards.back: Hard, fixed, non-tender, persistent enlargement or generalized unexplained lymphadenopathy.

cards.front: What are Reed-Sternberg cells classically associated with?
cards.back: Hodgkin lymphoma.

cards.front: What is a classic Reed-Sternberg appearance?
cards.back: Large binucleate/bilobed cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli ('owl eyes').

cards.front: What is the basic distinction between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma spread?
cards.back: Hodgkin often spreads contiguously; NHL more often shows noncontiguous/extranodal involvement.

cards.front: Why is node architecture important in lymphoma diagnosis?
cards.back: Malignant lymphoid proliferations often efface normal architecture.

cards.front: What is granulomatous lymphadenitis?
cards.back: Lymph-node inflammation characterized by granuloma formation.

cards.front: What is a common benign cause of tender lymph nodes?
cards.back: Acute infection/inflammation.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pathology
decks.title: Atherosclerosis

cards.front: What is atherosclerosis?
cards.back: Intimal plaques with lipid cores and fibrous caps in large and medium arteries.

cards.front: What is the initiating concept in atherogenesis?
cards.back: Endothelial injury/dysfunction leading to lipid entry, inflammation, and smooth-muscle responses.

cards.front: Which lipoprotein is most strongly implicated in atheroma formation?
cards.back: LDL, especially oxidized/modified LDL in the arterial intima.

cards.front: What are foam cells?
cards.back: Lipid-laden macrophages (and some smooth-muscle cells) within atherosclerotic lesions.

cards.front: What is a fatty streak?
cards.back: An early intimal lesion composed mainly of foam cells.

cards.front: What forms the fibrous cap of an atherosclerotic plaque?
cards.back: Smooth-muscle cells and extracellular matrix, especially collagen.

cards.front: What makes a plaque vulnerable to rupture?
cards.back: Thin fibrous cap, large lipid core, and active inflammation.

cards.front: Why is plaque rupture dangerous?
cards.back: It exposes thrombogenic material and can trigger acute occlusive thrombosis.

cards.front: What are major modifiable atherosclerosis risk factors?
cards.back: Hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking, and diabetes.

cards.front: What vascular complication can chronic atherosclerosis promote besides thrombosis?
cards.back: Aneurysm due to weakening/atrophy of the underlying media.

cards.front: Which arteries are commonly affected by atherosclerosis?
cards.back: Abdominal aorta, coronary, popliteal, internal carotid, and circle of Willis vessels.

cards.front: How does a stable plaque usually cause symptoms?
cards.back: Progressive stenosis limits flow, especially during increased tissue demand.

decks.subject: Microbiology
decks.title: Sepsis

cards.front: What is sepsis?
cards.back: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.

cards.front: What is septic shock?
cards.back: Sepsis with profound circulatory/metabolic abnormalities, typically requiring vasopressors despite fluids and associated with elevated lactate.

cards.front: What happens to systemic vascular resistance early in septic shock?
cards.back: It commonly decreases because of widespread vasodilation.

cards.front: Why can tissue hypoperfusion occur despite high cardiac output in early sepsis?
cards.back: Maldistributed microvascular flow and vasodilation impair effective oxygen delivery.

cards.front: What is a major role of bacterial endotoxin in sepsis?
cards.back: It activates innate immune pathways and promotes cytokine release.

cards.front: Which inflammatory mediators are prominent in sepsis?
cards.back: TNF, IL-1, IL-6 and other cytokines/mediators.

cards.front: Why can DIC occur in severe sepsis?
cards.back: Inflammation activates coagulation and suppresses anticoagulant/fibrinolytic pathways.

cards.front: What is a common metabolic marker of poor perfusion in sepsis?
cards.back: Elevated serum lactate.

cards.front: Why are blood cultures ideally obtained before antibiotics?
cards.back: To identify the pathogen without delaying urgent antimicrobial therapy.

cards.front: What is a key early treatment principle in suspected sepsis?
cards.back: Prompt antimicrobials plus source control and hemodynamic support.

cards.front: What is source control?
cards.back: Removing/draining the infectious focus, such as abscess drainage or infected-device removal.

cards.front: Why can multiple organs fail in sepsis?
cards.back: Systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, microthrombi, and hypoperfusion damage organs.

decks.subject: Microbiology
decks.title: Autoimmune Diseases

cards.front: What is autoimmunity?
cards.back: An immune response directed against self-antigens because self-tolerance fails.

cards.front: What is central tolerance?
cards.back: Elimination or editing of strongly self-reactive lymphocytes during development.

cards.front: What is peripheral tolerance?
cards.back: Mechanisms that suppress or inactivate self-reactive lymphocytes that escape central tolerance.

cards.front: What are regulatory T cells important for?
cards.back: Suppressing autoreactive immune responses and maintaining peripheral tolerance.

cards.front: How can molecular mimicry promote autoimmunity?
cards.back: Microbial antigens resemble self-antigens, causing cross-reactive immune responses.

cards.front: What is SLE?
cards.back: A systemic autoimmune disease with autoantibodies and immune-complex-mediated tissue injury.

cards.front: What antibody is highly specific for SLE?
cards.back: Anti-Smith antibody.

cards.front: What antibodies can be seen in SLE and correlate with disease activity/nephritis?
cards.back: Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies.

cards.front: What is rheumatoid arthritis primarily directed against?
cards.back: It is a systemic autoimmune inflammatory disease targeting synovial joints among other tissues.

cards.front: What is type III hypersensitivity's role in many autoimmune diseases?
cards.back: Immune complexes deposit in tissues and activate complement/inflammation.

cards.front: What is an organ-specific autoimmune disease example?
cards.back: Type 1 diabetes mellitus, Hashimoto thyroiditis, or Graves disease.

cards.front: Why are autoimmune diseases often chronic?
cards.back: Persistent self-antigens continually stimulate autoreactive immune responses.

decks.subject: Microbiology
decks.title: Immunodeficiency

cards.front: What is primary immunodeficiency?
cards.back: An inherited or developmental defect of immune function.

cards.front: What is secondary immunodeficiency?
cards.back: Acquired immune dysfunction from conditions such as HIV, malnutrition, cancer, or immunosuppressive therapy.

cards.front: What infections suggest a B-cell/antibody defect?
cards.back: Recurrent infections with encapsulated pyogenic bacteria, especially after maternal IgG wanes.

cards.front: What infections suggest a T-cell defect?
cards.back: Severe or recurrent viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections.

cards.front: What is SCID?
cards.back: Severe combined immunodeficiency affecting both cellular and humoral immunity.

cards.front: What is X-linked agammaglobulinemia caused by?
cards.back: BTK mutation causing failure of B-cell maturation.

cards.front: What is CVID characterized by?
cards.back: Low immunoglobulins with impaired antibody responses, often presenting later than XLA.

cards.front: What is selective IgA deficiency?
cards.back: Low/absent IgA with generally normal other immunoglobulins; may cause mucosal infections.

cards.front: What is DiGeorge syndrome's immune defect?
cards.back: Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia causing T-cell deficiency.

cards.front: What immune defect occurs in chronic granulomatous disease?
cards.back: Defective NADPH oxidase impairs respiratory burst in phagocytes.

cards.front: Which organisms are especially problematic in CGD?
cards.back: Catalase-positive organisms.

cards.front: What complement deficiency predisposes to Neisseria infection?
cards.back: Deficiency of terminal complement components C5–C9.

decks.subject: Microbiology
decks.title: Lymphatic Filariasis

cards.front: What organisms commonly cause lymphatic filariasis?
cards.back: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori.

cards.front: How is lymphatic filariasis transmitted?
cards.back: By mosquito vectors.

cards.front: Where do adult filarial worms live?
cards.back: Lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes.

cards.front: What are microfilariae?
cards.back: Larval forms that circulate in blood and can be taken up by mosquitoes.

cards.front: Why may blood collection timing matter in filariasis?
cards.back: Some species show nocturnal periodicity of microfilariae.

cards.front: What chronic complication can lymphatic obstruction cause?
cards.back: Lymphedema and elephantiasis.

cards.front: What male genital complication is classic with Wuchereria bancrofti?
cards.back: Hydrocele.

cards.front: What causes much of the chronic tissue damage in lymphatic filariasis?
cards.back: Inflammation and lymphatic dysfunction around adult worms and recurrent infection.

cards.front: What is a common diagnostic approach?
cards.back: Detection of microfilariae in blood or circulating filarial antigen, depending on species/testing availability.

cards.front: What does eosinophilia suggest in helminth infection?
cards.back: A Th2/eosinophil response to tissue-invasive parasites.

cards.front: Which immune response is prominent against helminths?
cards.back: Th2 immunity with IgE, mast cells, and eosinophils.

cards.front: Why can chronic filariasis produce massive swelling?
cards.back: Long-standing lymphatic obstruction and fibrosis impair lymph drainage.

decks.subject: Microbiology
decks.title: Hypersensitivity Part II

cards.front: What defines type III hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Tissue injury caused by deposition of antigen-antibody immune complexes.

cards.front: What activates inflammation after immune-complex deposition?
cards.back: Complement activation and recruitment of neutrophils.

cards.front: What is a classic systemic type III reaction?
cards.back: Serum sickness.

cards.front: What is a classic localized type III reaction?
cards.back: Arthus reaction.

cards.front: What autoimmune disease commonly involves type III mechanisms?
cards.back: Systemic lupus erythematosus.

cards.front: What defines type IV hypersensitivity?
cards.back: T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity rather than antibody-mediated injury.

cards.front: Which cells mediate delayed type IV reactions?
cards.back: Sensitized T lymphocytes, especially Th1/Th17 cells and sometimes CD8⁺ T cells.

cards.front: Why is type IV called delayed hypersensitivity?
cards.back: The reaction typically develops over 24–72 hours rather than minutes.

cards.front: What is a classic type IV test reaction?
cards.back: Tuberculin skin test.

cards.front: What is contact dermatitis an example of?
cards.back: Type IV hypersensitivity.

cards.front: How can CD8⁺ T cells cause type IV injury?
cards.back: They directly kill antigen-bearing target cells.

cards.front: What is the key contrast between type III and type IV hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Type III is immune-complex/complement mediated; type IV is T-cell mediated.

decks.subject: Microbiology
decks.title: Hypersensitivity Part I

cards.front: What is type I hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Immediate IgE-mediated mast-cell hypersensitivity.

cards.front: What happens during sensitization in type I hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Th2 responses drive IgE production; IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells.

cards.front: What triggers mast-cell degranulation in type I hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Allergen cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE.

cards.front: What mediator causes rapid vasodilation and increased vascular permeability in type I reactions?
cards.back: Histamine.

cards.front: What is anaphylaxis?
cards.back: A severe systemic immediate hypersensitivity reaction that can cause airway compromise and shock.

cards.front: What is the first-line emergency treatment for anaphylaxis?
cards.back: Intramuscular epinephrine.

cards.front: What is type II hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Antibody-mediated injury against cell-surface or extracellular-matrix antigens.

cards.front: Which immunoglobulins usually mediate type II hypersensitivity?
cards.back: IgG or IgM.

cards.front: How can type II antibodies damage cells?
cards.back: Opsonization/phagocytosis, complement activation, inflammation, or receptor dysfunction.

cards.front: What is an example of type II cytotoxic disease?
cards.back: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

cards.front: How can type II antibodies cause disease without destroying cells?
cards.back: They can stimulate or block receptors, as in Graves disease or myasthenia gravis.

cards.front: What is the key difference between type I and type II hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Type I is IgE/mast-cell immediate allergy; type II uses IgG/IgM against specific tissue targets.

decks.subject: Microbiology
decks.title: Babesiosis and Malaria II

cards.front: What is Babesia?
cards.back: An intraerythrocytic protozoan parasite transmitted mainly by Ixodes ticks.

cards.front: What blood-smear finding is classic for babesiosis?
cards.back: Maltese-cross tetrads may be seen in RBCs.

cards.front: How does babesiosis differ from malaria epidemiologically?
cards.back: Babesia is tick-borne; malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes.

cards.front: Which patients are at higher risk for severe babesiosis?
cards.back: Asplenic, older, or immunocompromised patients.

cards.front: What major hematologic effect can babesiosis cause?
cards.back: Hemolytic anemia.

cards.front: Which malaria species have dormant liver hypnozoites?
cards.back: Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale.

cards.front: Why can P. vivax and P. ovale relapse?
cards.back: Dormant hypnozoites can reactivate from the liver.

cards.front: Which malaria species is most associated with severe/cerebral malaria?
cards.back: Plasmodium falciparum.

cards.front: Why is falciparum malaria especially severe?
cards.back: Infected RBCs adhere to endothelium and sequester in microvasculature.

cards.front: What is the definitive host of Plasmodium?
cards.back: The female Anopheles mosquito, where sexual reproduction occurs.

cards.front: What stage infects humans from the mosquito?
cards.back: Sporozoites.

cards.front: What stage infects mosquitoes from humans?
cards.back: Gametocytes.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Microbiology
decks.title: Malaria I

cards.front: How is malaria transmitted?
cards.back: By the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.

cards.front: What is the first human stage after mosquito inoculation?
cards.back: Sporozoites enter blood and invade hepatocytes.

cards.front: What happens during the hepatic stage of malaria?
cards.back: Sporozoites develop into schizonts that release merozoites into blood.

cards.front: What happens during the erythrocytic stage?
cards.back: Merozoites invade RBCs and develop through ring/trophozoite and schizont stages.

cards.front: What causes periodic fever in malaria?
cards.back: Synchronous rupture of infected RBCs and release of merozoites/inflammatory products.

cards.front: Which malaria species can infect RBCs of all ages?
cards.back: Plasmodium falciparum.

cards.front: Why can falciparum parasitemia become very high?
cards.back: It can invade RBCs of all ages rather than a restricted subset.

cards.front: Which species prefers reticulocytes?
cards.back: P. vivax and P. ovale.

cards.front: Which species prefers older RBCs?
cards.back: P. malariae.

cards.front: What is the characteristic RBC morphology in falciparum malaria?
cards.back: Multiple delicate ring forms may occur; crescent/banana-shaped gametocytes are characteristic.

cards.front: What is the main diagnostic test for malaria?
cards.back: Microscopic examination of thick and thin peripheral blood smears.

cards.front: Why are both thick and thin smears useful?
cards.back: Thick smear increases sensitivity; thin smear helps species identification and parasitemia estimation.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Antianginal Drugs

cards.front: What is the main goal of antianginal therapy?
cards.back: Reduce myocardial O₂ demand and/or improve coronary O₂ supply.

cards.front: How do nitrates relieve angina?
cards.back: Venodilation lowers preload and ventricular wall stress, reducing myocardial O₂ demand.

cards.front: What intracellular mediator causes nitrate-induced smooth-muscle relaxation?
cards.back: Nitric oxide increases cGMP.

cards.front: What common adverse effect occurs with nitrates?
cards.back: Headache from vasodilation.

cards.front: Why must nitrates not be combined with PDE-5 inhibitors?
cards.back: The combination can cause profound hypotension through excessive cGMP.

cards.front: How do beta blockers reduce anginal symptoms?
cards.back: They lower heart rate and contractility, reducing O₂ demand and prolonging diastole.

cards.front: Why are beta blockers useful in chronic stable angina?
cards.back: They blunt exercise-induced increases in heart rate and contractility.

cards.front: How do non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers help angina?
cards.back: They reduce heart rate/contractility and dilate coronary/systemic arteries.

cards.front: How do dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers help angina?
cards.back: They predominantly cause arterial vasodilation, lowering afterload and improving coronary flow.

cards.front: What is the main concern with combining a beta blocker and verapamil?
cards.back: Excessive bradycardia, AV block, and depressed contractility.

cards.front: How does ranolazine help chronic angina?
cards.back: It inhibits late Na⁺ current, reducing diastolic wall tension and O₂ demand with little effect on HR/BP.

cards.front: Which antianginal class is especially useful for vasospastic angina?
cards.back: Calcium-channel blockers; nitrates also relieve spasm.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Antihyperlipidemic Drugs

cards.front: What enzyme do statins inhibit?
cards.back: HMG-CoA reductase.

cards.front: How do statins lower plasma LDL?
cards.back: Reduced hepatic cholesterol increases LDL-receptor expression and LDL clearance.

cards.front: What major lipid effect do statins produce?
cards.back: Large reduction in LDL cholesterol.

cards.front: What important adverse effects should be remembered with statins?
cards.back: Myopathy and elevated liver enzymes; severe rhabdomyolysis is rare.

cards.front: How does ezetimibe lower cholesterol?
cards.back: It inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption via NPC1L1.

cards.front: How do bile-acid sequestrants lower LDL?
cards.back: They bind bile acids in the gut, forcing hepatic cholesterol use and increasing LDL receptors.

cards.front: What lipid abnormality are fibrates especially useful for?
cards.back: Hypertriglyceridemia.

cards.front: How do fibrates work?
cards.back: They activate PPAR-α, increasing lipoprotein lipase activity and fatty-acid oxidation.

cards.front: What is a notable fibrate adverse effect?
cards.back: Gallstones and myopathy risk, especially with some statin combinations.

cards.front: How do PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL?
cards.back: They prevent LDL-receptor degradation, increasing receptor recycling and LDL clearance.

cards.front: What is niacin's main lipid effect?
cards.back: It lowers VLDL/TG and can raise HDL, though its use is limited by adverse effects.

cards.front: Why is severe hypertriglyceridemia treated aggressively?
cards.back: Very high triglycerides increase acute pancreatitis risk.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Immune Suppressants and Immune Modulators

cards.front: What is the major mechanism of glucocorticoid immunosuppression?
cards.back: Broad suppression of inflammatory gene transcription and cytokine production.

cards.front: What do calcineurin inhibitors suppress?
cards.back: IL-2 transcription and T-cell activation.

cards.front: Name two calcineurin inhibitors.
cards.back: Cyclosporine and tacrolimus.

cards.front: What major toxicity is shared by cyclosporine and tacrolimus?
cards.back: Nephrotoxicity.

cards.front: How does sirolimus suppress T cells?
cards.back: It inhibits mTOR, blocking response to IL-2 and T-cell proliferation.

cards.front: How does mycophenolate suppress lymphocytes?
cards.back: It inhibits IMP dehydrogenase and de novo guanine synthesis, especially affecting lymphocytes.

cards.front: How does azathioprine work?
cards.back: It is converted to 6-mercaptopurine metabolites that inhibit purine synthesis.

cards.front: What is methotrexate's immunomodulatory target?
cards.back: It inhibits folate-dependent nucleotide metabolism and has anti-inflammatory effects at low doses.

cards.front: What is a major use of biologic anti-TNF therapy?
cards.back: Inflammatory autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease.

cards.front: What infection risk must be considered before anti-TNF therapy?
cards.back: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis.

cards.front: What does rituximab target?
cards.back: CD20 on B cells.

cards.front: What is a general consequence of immunosuppressive therapy?
cards.back: Increased susceptibility to infection and some malignancies.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Pharmacology of Hypersensitivity

cards.front: What is first-line treatment for anaphylaxis?
cards.back: Intramuscular epinephrine.

cards.front: Why is epinephrine effective in anaphylaxis?
cards.back: α1 vasoconstriction raises BP/reduces edema; β1 supports heart; β2 bronchodilates and reduces mediator release.

cards.front: What receptor do H1 antihistamines block?
cards.back: Histamine H1 receptors.

cards.front: What symptoms are H1 antihistamines best at treating?
cards.back: Histamine-mediated itching, sneezing, urticaria, and rhinorrhea.

cards.front: Why are antihistamines not a substitute for epinephrine in anaphylaxis?
cards.back: They do not rapidly reverse airway edema, bronchospasm, or shock.

cards.front: What distinguishes first-generation H1 blockers?
cards.back: They enter the CNS and commonly cause sedation and anticholinergic effects.

cards.front: What distinguishes second-generation H1 blockers?
cards.back: Less CNS penetration and therefore less sedation.

cards.front: How do corticosteroids help allergic disease?
cards.back: They suppress inflammatory gene expression and late-phase inflammation.

cards.front: Do corticosteroids act rapidly enough to replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis?
cards.back: No; their onset is too slow for immediate lifesaving treatment.

cards.front: What do leukotriene receptor antagonists block?
cards.back: Cysteinyl leukotriene effects involved in bronchoconstriction and inflammation.

cards.front: What is omalizumab's target?
cards.back: Free IgE, reducing IgE-mediated mast-cell activation.

cards.front: What is the pharmacologic priority in severe acute hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Stabilize airway, breathing, and circulation; give IM epinephrine promptly.

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Drugs Affecting Hemostasis and Coagulation

cards.front: How does unfractionated heparin act?
cards.back: It accelerates antithrombin inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa.

cards.front: Which test commonly monitors unfractionated heparin?
cards.back: aPTT.

cards.front: How do low-molecular-weight heparins differ from UFH?
cards.back: They inhibit factor Xa more selectively and have more predictable pharmacokinetics.

cards.front: What antidote reverses heparin?
cards.back: Protamine sulfate.

cards.front: How does warfarin work?
cards.back: It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing activation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S.

cards.front: Which test monitors warfarin?
cards.back: PT/INR.

cards.front: Why can warfarin initially be prothrombotic?
cards.back: Protein C falls rapidly before several procoagulant factors, creating transient hypercoagulability.

cards.front: What are direct factor Xa inhibitors examples?
cards.back: Apixaban and rivaroxaban.

cards.front: What is a direct thrombin inhibitor example?
cards.back: Dabigatran.

cards.front: How do thrombolytics work?
cards.back: They increase plasmin generation and promote fibrin clot breakdown.

cards.front: What major risk is shared by anticoagulants and thrombolytics?
cards.back: Bleeding.

cards.front: What is vitamin K used for pharmacologically?
cards.back: To reverse or treat vitamin K antagonist effect/deficiency when clinically appropriate.

decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Treatment of Anemia

cards.front: What is first-line replacement for uncomplicated iron-deficiency anemia?
cards.back: Oral iron, if tolerated and absorption is adequate.

cards.front: Where is oral iron best absorbed?
cards.back: Duodenum and proximal jejunum.

cards.front: What common adverse effects occur with oral iron?
cards.back: GI upset, constipation, abdominal discomfort, and dark stools.

cards.front: When may IV iron be preferred?
cards.back: Severe deficiency needing rapid replacement, malabsorption, ongoing losses, or intolerance of oral iron.

cards.front: What treats folate-deficiency megaloblastic anemia?
cards.back: Folic acid replacement.

cards.front: Why must vitamin B12 deficiency be excluded before giving folate alone?
cards.back: Folate can improve anemia while neurologic B12 injury progresses.

cards.front: How is vitamin B12 deficiency treated?
cards.back: Vitamin B12 replacement, orally at adequate dose or parenterally when needed.

cards.front: What does erythropoietin therapy stimulate?
cards.back: Erythroid progenitor proliferation and RBC production.

cards.front: A common indication for erythropoiesis-stimulating agents?
cards.back: Anemia of chronic kidney disease.

cards.front: What substrate should be adequate for EPO therapy to work well?
cards.back: Iron stores.

cards.front: What major risks occur with excessive erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy?
cards.back: Hypertension and thromboembolic/cardiovascular events.

cards.front: What determines anemia treatment?
cards.back: Correct the underlying cause and replace the specific missing substrate or stimulus.

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Pulmonary Embolism Management

cards.front: What is the main pharmacologic treatment for most acute pulmonary emboli?
cards.back: Anticoagulation.

cards.front: Why is anticoagulation used in PE?
cards.back: It prevents clot extension and new thrombosis while endogenous fibrinolysis resolves the embolus.

cards.front: Which parenteral anticoagulants may be used initially in PE?
cards.back: LMWH, unfractionated heparin, or fondaparinux depending on the clinical setting.

cards.front: Why might UFH be chosen in an unstable PE patient?
cards.back: Rapid onset/offset and reversibility are useful when procedures or thrombolysis may be needed.

cards.front: Which oral drugs are commonly used for ongoing PE anticoagulation?
cards.back: Direct oral anticoagulants or warfarin, depending on patient factors.

cards.front: When is systemic thrombolysis considered in PE?
cards.back: Primarily in high-risk PE with hemodynamic instability, if bleeding risk permits.

cards.front: What is the major danger of thrombolysis?
cards.back: Major bleeding, especially intracranial hemorrhage.

cards.front: What is a key alternative when thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails in severe PE?
cards.back: Catheter-based therapy or surgical embolectomy in selected patients.

cards.front: What is the role of an IVC filter?
cards.back: Selected patients with acute VTE who cannot receive anticoagulation, or rare recurrent events despite adequate therapy.

cards.front: What determines duration of anticoagulation after PE?
cards.back: Whether PE was provoked/unprovoked, recurrence risk, bleeding risk, and persistent risk factors.

cards.front: Why should hemodynamic status be assessed immediately in PE?
cards.back: It separates high-risk unstable PE from lower-risk presentations and guides reperfusion decisions.

cards.front: What supportive treatment may be needed in severe PE?
cards.back: Oxygen and careful circulatory/vasopressor support when shock is present.

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Antiplatelet Drugs

cards.front: How does aspirin inhibit platelets?
cards.back: It irreversibly inhibits COX-1, reducing thromboxane A₂ synthesis.

cards.front: Why does aspirin's platelet effect last for the platelet lifespan?
cards.back: Platelets cannot synthesize new COX because they lack nuclei.

cards.front: What do P2Y12 inhibitors block?
cards.back: ADP-mediated platelet activation through the P2Y12 receptor.

cards.front: Name common oral P2Y12 inhibitors.
cards.back: Clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticagrelor.

cards.front: What is clopidogrel?
cards.back: A prodrug P2Y12 inhibitor requiring hepatic activation.

cards.front: What is the final common receptor for platelet aggregation?
cards.back: GPIIb/IIIa, which binds fibrinogen.

cards.front: What do GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors do?
cards.back: Block the final common pathway of platelet aggregation.

cards.front: Why are antiplatelet drugs especially useful in arterial thrombosis?
cards.back: Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich because of high shear stress.

cards.front: What is dual antiplatelet therapy commonly composed of?
cards.back: Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor.

cards.front: What is the major adverse effect of antiplatelet therapy?
cards.back: Bleeding.

cards.front: How does dipyridamole reduce platelet activation?
cards.back: It increases platelet cAMP/cGMP signaling partly through phosphodiesterase inhibition and adenosine effects.

cards.front: How does cilostazol work?
cards.back: PDE3 inhibition increases cAMP, inhibiting platelets and causing vasodilation.

decks.subject: Anatomy
decks.title: CVS Radiology

cards.front: What is the standard chest radiograph view used to assess heart size in ambulatory adults?
cards.back: Posteroanterior (PA) view.

cards.front: Why can an AP chest radiograph exaggerate heart size?
cards.back: The heart is farther from the detector and is magnified.

cards.front: What is cardiomegaly on a PA chest X-ray commonly assessed by?
cards.back: A cardiothoracic ratio greater than about 50%.

cards.front: Which chamber contributes most to the left lower cardiac border on PA CXR?
cards.back: Left ventricle.

cards.front: Which chamber forms most of the right cardiac border?
cards.back: Right atrium.

cards.front: What structure forms the upper right mediastinal contour?
cards.back: Superior vena cava.

cards.front: What structure contributes to the left upper mediastinal contour?
cards.back: Aortic arch/knob.

cards.front: What does pulmonary vascular congestion suggest?
cards.back: Elevated pulmonary venous pressure, commonly from left-sided heart failure.

cards.front: What can a widened mediastinum suggest in the right clinical context?
cards.back: Aortic pathology such as aneurysm/dissection, among other causes.

cards.front: What imaging modality gives rapid cross-sectional assessment of great vessels?
cards.back: CT, particularly CT angiography for vascular anatomy.

cards.front: What imaging modality is first-line for dynamic valve and ventricular function?
cards.back: Echocardiography.

cards.front: What is cardiac MRI particularly useful for?
cards.back: Detailed anatomy, ventricular function, tissue characterization, and congenital/cardiomyopathy assessment.

decks.subject: Anatomy
decks.title: Mediastinum and Pericardium

cards.front: What divides the superior and inferior mediastinum?
cards.back: A transverse plane from the sternal angle to the T4/T5 intervertebral level.

cards.front: What subdivisions make up the inferior mediastinum?
cards.back: Anterior, middle, and posterior mediastina.

cards.front: Where is the heart located within the mediastinum?
cards.back: Middle mediastinum.

cards.front: What are the layers of the pericardium?
cards.back: Fibrous pericardium and serous pericardium; serous has parietal and visceral layers.

cards.front: What is the visceral layer of serous pericardium called?
cards.back: Epicardium.

cards.front: Where is the pericardial cavity?
cards.back: Between parietal and visceral serous pericardium.

cards.front: What is the transverse pericardial sinus located between?
cards.back: Arterial outflow (aorta/pulmonary trunk) and venous inflow structures.

cards.front: What is the oblique pericardial sinus?
cards.back: A blind recess posterior to the left atrium between pulmonary veins/IVC reflections.

cards.front: What nerve provides sensory innervation to fibrous and parietal pericardium?
cards.back: Phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

cards.front: Where can pericardial pain be referred?
cards.back: Shoulder/supraclavicular region via C3–C5 dermatomes.

cards.front: What anchors fibrous pericardium inferiorly?
cards.back: Central tendon of the diaphragm.

cards.front: Why is rapid pericardial fluid accumulation dangerous?
cards.back: It can compress the heart and impair diastolic filling, causing tamponade.
