decks.subject: Anatomy
decks.title: External Features of the Heart

cards.front: Which chamber forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart?
cards.back: Right ventricle.

cards.front: Which chamber forms most of the base/posterior surface?
cards.back: Left atrium.

cards.front: Which chamber forms the apex?
cards.back: Left ventricle.

cards.front: Where is the apex beat normally found?
cards.back: Left 5th intercostal space near the midclavicular line.

cards.front: Which chamber forms most of the right border of the heart?
cards.back: Right atrium.

cards.front: Which chamber forms most of the left border?
cards.back: Left ventricle, with contribution from the left auricle.

cards.front: What separates atria from ventricles externally?
cards.back: Coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus.

cards.front: What do interventricular grooves mark?
cards.back: External position of the interventricular septum.

cards.front: Which coronary artery runs in the anterior interventricular groove?
cards.back: Anterior interventricular (LAD) artery.

cards.front: Which major vein accompanies the LAD?
cards.back: Great cardiac vein.

cards.front: Which artery often runs in the posterior interventricular groove?
cards.back: Posterior interventricular artery, commonly from the RCA in right dominance.

cards.front: What does coronary dominance refer to?
cards.back: Which coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.

decks.subject: Anatomy
decks.title: Internal Features of the Heart

cards.front: What structures characterize the right atrium internally?
cards.back: Pectinate muscles anteriorly, smooth sinus venarum posteriorly, and fossa ovalis on septum.

cards.front: What separates smooth and rough parts of the right atrium internally?
cards.back: Crista terminalis.

cards.front: What is the fossa ovalis?
cards.back: A depression in the interatrial septum marking the fetal foramen ovale.

cards.front: What valve lies between right atrium and right ventricle?
cards.back: Tricuspid valve.

cards.front: What are chordae tendineae attached to?
cards.back: AV valve cusps and papillary muscles.

cards.front: What is the purpose of papillary muscles?
cards.back: They tense chordae during systole and prevent AV valve prolapse.

cards.front: What muscular structure is characteristic of the right ventricle?
cards.back: Trabeculae carneae; the moderator band is also distinctive.

cards.front: What does the moderator band carry?
cards.back: Part of the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle/right ventricular wall.

cards.front: What valve lies between left atrium and left ventricle?
cards.back: Mitral (bicuspid) valve.

cards.front: Why is the left ventricular wall thicker than the right?
cards.back: It pumps against much higher systemic vascular resistance.

cards.front: What are the semilunar valves?
cards.back: Aortic and pulmonary valves.

cards.front: Where are the coronary artery openings located?
cards.back: In the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve cusps.

decks.subject: Histology
decks.title: Histology of the Lymphatic System

cards.front: What is the basic structural framework of many lymphoid organs?
cards.back: Reticular connective tissue supporting lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells.

cards.front: What are primary lymphoid organs?
cards.back: Sites of lymphocyte development/maturation: bone marrow and thymus.

cards.front: What are secondary lymphoid organs?
cards.back: Sites where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen, such as lymph nodes, spleen, and MALT.

cards.front: What is the outer region of a lymph node called?
cards.back: Cortex.

cards.front: Where are B-cell follicles mainly located in a lymph node?
cards.back: Cortex.

cards.front: What is a germinal center?
cards.back: A site of activated B-cell proliferation, selection, and differentiation within a secondary follicle.

cards.front: Where are T cells concentrated in a lymph node?
cards.back: Paracortex.

cards.front: What is found in the lymph-node medulla?
cards.back: Medullary cords containing plasma cells/lymphocytes and medullary sinuses.

cards.front: Where do afferent lymphatics enter a lymph node?
cards.back: Through the convex surface.

cards.front: Where does the efferent lymphatic leave a lymph node?
cards.back: At the hilum.

cards.front: What is a key histologic feature of thymus?
cards.back: Lobules with dark cortex and lighter medulla; no lymphoid follicles.

cards.front: What are Hassall corpuscles?
cards.back: Concentric eosinophilic epithelial-reticular structures in the thymic medulla.

decks.subject: Histology
decks.title: Histology of Mucosal Lymphatic Tissue

cards.front: What does MALT stand for?
cards.back: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.

cards.front: What is the purpose of MALT?
cards.back: Local immune surveillance and response at mucosal surfaces.

cards.front: Give major examples of organized MALT.
cards.back: Tonsils, Peyer patches, and appendix.

cards.front: Where are Peyer patches found?
cards.back: Primarily in the ileum.

cards.front: What are M cells?
cards.back: Specialized epithelial cells that sample luminal antigens and deliver them to underlying immune cells.

cards.front: Which immunoglobulin is especially important in mucosal immunity?
cards.back: Secretory IgA.

cards.front: What is GALT?
cards.back: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue, a major component of MALT.

cards.front: What distinguishes a lymphoid nodule from diffuse lymphoid tissue?
cards.back: A nodule is a localized dense collection, often with a germinal center when activated.

cards.front: What tonsillar feature increases antigen exposure?
cards.back: Epithelial invaginations called crypts, especially prominent in palatine tonsils.

cards.front: Which tonsil is lined mainly by stratified squamous epithelium?
cards.back: Palatine tonsil.

cards.front: Which tonsil is lined mainly by respiratory epithelium?
cards.back: Pharyngeal tonsil.

cards.front: Why is MALT strategically located beneath epithelia?
cards.back: Mucosal surfaces are major entry sites for pathogens and foreign antigens.

decks.subject: Histology
decks.title: Histology of Myocardium

cards.front: What type of muscle forms the myocardium?
cards.back: Cardiac muscle.

cards.front: How are cardiac muscle cells arranged?
cards.back: Branched striated cells connected end-to-end by intercalated discs.

cards.front: How many nuclei do cardiomyocytes usually have?
cards.back: One central nucleus, sometimes two.

cards.front: What are intercalated discs?
cards.back: Specialized junctional complexes connecting adjacent cardiomyocytes mechanically and electrically.

cards.front: Which junction in intercalated discs allows electrical coupling?
cards.back: Gap junctions.

cards.front: Which junctions provide strong mechanical attachment between cardiomyocytes?
cards.back: Desmosomes and fascia adherens.

cards.front: Why are cardiomyocytes rich in mitochondria?
cards.back: They require continuous aerobic ATP production for rhythmic contraction.

cards.front: What surrounds individual cardiac muscle fibers?
cards.back: A delicate endomysium rich in capillaries.

cards.front: What are Purkinje fibers?
cards.back: Specialized conducting cardiomyocytes located mainly in the subendocardium.

cards.front: How do Purkinje fibers look histologically compared with working myocytes?
cards.back: Larger, paler cells with fewer peripheral myofibrils and more glycogen.

cards.front: What layer lines the chambers of the heart?
cards.back: Endocardium.

cards.front: What layer covers the external heart surface?
cards.back: Epicardium, the visceral layer of serous pericardium.

decks.subject: Pharmacology
decks.title: Antihypertensive Drugs

cards.front: How do baroreceptors provide rapid blood-pressure control?
cards.back: They sense arterial-pressure changes and alter autonomic activity, changing heart rate, contractility, and vascular tone.

cards.front: How does the RAAS raise blood pressure long term?
cards.back: Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction (↑ peripheral resistance), while aldosterone retains Na⁺/water (↑ blood volume → ↑ stroke volume and cardiac output).

cards.front: Which lifestyle measure generally produces the greatest blood-pressure reduction?
cards.back: Weight loss toward a healthy body weight.

cards.front: Which drug classes are first-line options for uncomplicated hypertension?
cards.back: ACE inhibitor or ARB, thiazide-type diuretic, and calcium-channel blocker.

cards.front: Why are ACE inhibitors or ARBs preferred in diabetes with albuminuria or CKD?
cards.back: They provide nephroprotection in addition to lowering blood pressure.

cards.front: A patient develops a persistent dry cough on lisinopril. What is the preferred switch?
cards.back: Switch to an ARB such as losartan; ARBs do not increase bradykinin and therefore avoid the classic ACE-inhibitor cough.

cards.front: What adverse effects are shared by ACE inhibitors and ARBs?
cards.back: Hyperkalemia and increased creatinine; both require potassium and renal-function monitoring.

cards.front: When should ACE inhibitors and ARBs be avoided?
cards.back: Pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis.

cards.front: Where do thiazide diuretics act?
cards.back: At the distal convoluted tubule, inhibiting the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter.

cards.front: What are the high-yield electrolyte/metabolic effects of thiazides?
cards.back: ↓Na⁺, ↓K⁺, ↑uric acid, ↑glucose, and ↑Ca²⁺.

cards.front: Why do thiazides remain effective for chronic hypertension after the initial volume effect?
cards.back: Long term they reduce vascular smooth-muscle reactivity, causing arteriolar relaxation and decreased peripheral resistance.

cards.front: Where do loop diuretics act and what transporter do they inhibit?
cards.back: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle; they inhibit NKCC2.

cards.front: What are major adverse effects of loop diuretics?
cards.back: Hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, ototoxicity, dehydration, and volume depletion.

cards.front: When are loop diuretics particularly useful in hypertension?
cards.back: When volume control is needed, especially symptomatic heart failure or advanced CKD (particularly GFR <30 mL/min).

cards.front: What is the role of spironolactone in hypertension?
cards.back: It antagonizes the aldosterone receptor and is a common add-on for resistant hypertension; it is also useful in primary hyperaldosteronism and HFrEF.

cards.front: What important adverse effects are associated with spironolactone?
cards.back: Hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.

cards.front: Which potassium-sparing drugs block ENaC and when may they be useful?
cards.back: Amiloride and triamterene; they can be added when thiazides cause or worsen hypokalemia. ENaC blockade is also useful in Liddle syndrome.

cards.front: Which antihypertensive combinations are commonly complementary?
cards.back: ACE inhibitor/ARB + DHP calcium-channel blocker, or ACE inhibitor/ARB + thiazide-type diuretic.

cards.front: Why should an ACE inhibitor and ARB not be combined routinely?
cards.back: Dual RAAS blockade increases renal dysfunction and hyperkalemia without routine added benefit.

cards.front: Why is a β-blocker plus verapamil or diltiazem used cautiously?
cards.back: The combination can cause severe bradycardia, AV block, and myocardial depression.

cards.front: When do β-blockers become preferred antihypertensive agents?
cards.back: When there is a compelling indication such as ischemic heart disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, thoracic aortic disease, thyrotoxicosis, migraine, or essential tremor.

cards.front: Which β-blockers are cardioselective vs nonselective?
cards.back: Cardioselective: atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate. Nonselective: nadolol, propranolol.

cards.front: Which antihypertensives may be useful in BPH or pheochromocytoma?
cards.back: α₁ blockers such as prazosin or doxazosin; they may help BPH symptoms and are used in hypertension due to pheochromocytoma.

cards.front: Which antihypertensive drugs are commonly used in pregnancy?
cards.back: Labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa, and hydralazine (especially for acute severe hypertension).

cards.front: Which antihypertensive classes are contraindicated in pregnancy?
cards.back: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and direct renin inhibitors because RAAS blockade can cause fetal toxicity, especially renal injury and oligohydramnios.

cards.front: How is initial drug therapy approached in stage 2 hypertension?
cards.back: If BP is >20/10 mmHg above target, start two first-line drugs from different classes; a single-pill combination is preferred when possible.

cards.front: For Black adults without heart failure or CKD, which classes should initial therapy include?
cards.back: A thiazide-type diuretic or calcium-channel blocker.

cards.front: What distinguishes hypertensive emergency from severe asymptomatic hypertension?
cards.back: Acute target-organ damage. Hypertensive emergency requires monitored care and titratable IV therapy; severe asymptomatic hypertension is generally lowered gradually with oral therapy.

cards.front: What is the usual initial BP-reduction goal in hypertensive emergency?
cards.back: Reduce mean arterial pressure by about 20–25% initially, then lower BP gradually, except where condition-specific targets apply.

cards.front: What is the preferred next drug after true resistant hypertension persists on an ARB/ACEI, amlodipine, and chlorthalidone?
cards.back: Spironolactone, if renal function and potassium permit.

cards.front: How soon should a patient generally be reviewed after starting antihypertensive medication?
cards.back: About 1 month to assess adherence, BP response, adverse effects, and relevant labs.

cards.front: In CKD, when should creatinine and potassium be checked after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB?
cards.back: Within 2–4 weeks.

cards.front: What is therapeutic inertia in hypertension?
cards.back: Failure to appropriately intensify treatment when blood pressure remains above target.

cards.front: What adverse effect suggests hydralazine-induced lupus?
cards.back: Arthralgia and fever with positive antinuclear antibodies after prolonged hydralazine use.

cards.front: Which vasodilator is classically associated with excessive hair growth?
cards.back: Minoxidil.

cards.front: Why should verapamil generally be avoided in HFrEF?
cards.back: Its negative inotropic effect can worsen systolic heart failure.

cards.front: Why can amlodipine cause ankle edema without pulmonary congestion?
cards.back: Preferential arteriolar dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, producing peripheral edema.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Cardiac Contractility
decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

cards.front: What mainly controls contraction in cardiac cells?
cards.back: Ca²⁺ influx.

cards.front: What is the direct effect of calcium-channel blockers on cardiac contractility?
cards.back: They reduce Ca²⁺ entry and have a negative inotropic effect.

cards.front: What is preload?
cards.back: The resting/initial length of cardiac muscle before contraction.

cards.front: What represents preload in the intact heart?
cards.back: End-diastolic volume (EDV).

cards.front: State the Frank-Starling relationship.
cards.back: Within limits, greater initial myocardial fiber length (preload) produces greater force of contraction.

cards.front: What is afterload?
cards.back: The load/resistance the contracting ventricle must overcome during ejection.

cards.front: What represents afterload in the intact left ventricle?
cards.back: Aortic pressure.

cards.front: How does increased afterload affect shortening velocity?
cards.back: It decreases the velocity of myocardial shortening.

cards.front: What are the three major factors affecting cardiac muscle performance in the lecture?
cards.back: Preload, afterload, and the inotropic state (contractility).

cards.front: How does sympathetic stimulation affect atrial contractility?
cards.back: It increases atrial contractility.

cards.front: How does sympathetic stimulation affect ventricular contractility?
cards.back: It increases ventricular contractility.

cards.front: How does parasympathetic stimulation affect atrial contractility?
cards.back: It decreases atrial contractility.

cards.front: How does parasympathetic stimulation affect ventricular contractility?
cards.back: The lecture lists no significant direct effect.

cards.front: How does sympathetic stimulation of veins affect preload?
cards.back: Venoconstriction increases venous return and preload.

cards.front: What is the approximate AV nodal delay?
cards.back: About 100 ms.

cards.front: Why is the AV nodal delay useful?
cards.back: It allows atrial depolarization/contraction and emptying before ventricular depolarization and contraction.

cards.front: How fast do Purkinje fibers conduct in the lecture?
cards.back: About 4 m/s.

cards.front: Why is rapid Purkinje conduction important?
cards.back: It activates ventricular muscle rapidly so ventricular fibers contract nearly simultaneously.

cards.front: What happens when preload rises through increased venous return?
cards.back: EDV and initial fiber length rise, increasing contraction force and stroke volume within limits.

cards.front: What happens to ventricular performance when afterload becomes very high?
cards.back: Shortening/force and cardiac output fall.

cards.front: Which autonomic division decreases AV nodal delay?
cards.back: Sympathetic stimulation.

cards.front: Which autonomic division increases AV nodal delay?
cards.back: Parasympathetic stimulation.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Cardiac Output and Its Control
decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

cards.front: What is stroke volume?
cards.back: The volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per beat; about 70 mL in the lecture example.

cards.front: What is cardiac output?
cards.back: The volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute.

cards.front: What is the cardiac output formula?
cards.back: CO = stroke volume × heart rate.

cards.front: What is a typical resting cardiac output in the lecture example?
cards.back: About 5 L/min (70 mL × 72 beats/min).

cards.front: What is ejection fraction?
cards.back: The fraction of EDV ejected as stroke volume.

cards.front: What is the ejection fraction formula?
cards.back: EF = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume.

cards.front: What normal EF does the lecture give?
cards.back: About 55%.

cards.front: What is EDV?
cards.back: The volume in a ventricle at the end of diastole; about 130 mL in the lecture.

cards.front: What is ESV?
cards.back: The volume remaining in a ventricle at the end of systole; about 60 mL in the lecture.

cards.front: How is stroke volume related to EDV and ESV?
cards.back: SV = EDV − ESV.

cards.front: How is EDV related to cardiac output?
cards.back: EDV/preload is directly related to stroke volume and cardiac output.

cards.front: How is ESV related to stroke volume and cardiac output?
cards.back: ESV is inversely related: greater contractility lowers ESV and raises SV/CO.

cards.front: What mainly determines preload?
cards.back: Venous return.

cards.front: State the Frank-Starling effect on cardiac output.
cards.back: More venous return → more EDV/preload → stronger contraction → greater SV and CO, within limits.

cards.front: What is afterload?
cards.back: The resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.

cards.front: Give three examples of afterload from the lecture.
cards.back: Aortic blood pressure, aortic valve stenosis, and peripheral resistance.

cards.front: How does hemorrhage affect venous return?
cards.back: It lowers blood volume and decreases venous return.

cards.front: How does sympathetic stimulation affect venous return?
cards.back: Venoconstriction increases venous return.

cards.front: How does standing affect venous return?
cards.back: Gravity decreases venous return from veins below the heart.

cards.front: How does inspiration affect venous return?
cards.back: The respiratory pump increases venous return during inspiration.

cards.front: How does very high HR (>180/min) affect cardiac output?
cards.back: It reduces ventricular filling/preload and can decrease cardiac output.

cards.front: Why can trained athletes reach higher maximal cardiac output?
cards.back: Mainly because they can generate a much larger stroke volume, not because of a much higher maximal HR.

decks.subject: Pathology
decks.title: Pathology of Hypertension
decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

cards.front: How is systemic hypertension defined in this lecture?
cards.back: A sustained increase in resting blood pressure above generally accepted normal levels.

cards.front: What proportion of hypertension is essential (primary)?
cards.back: About 90–95%; its cause is unknown.

cards.front: What are the main secondary hypertension categories listed?
cards.back: Renal, endocrine, vascular, and neurogenic causes.

cards.front: What vascular lesion is typical of benign hypertension?
cards.back: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis.

cards.front: What vascular lesion is typical of malignant hypertension?
cards.back: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.

cards.front: What clinical findings accompany malignant hypertension in the lecture?
cards.back: Rapidly rising BP with renal failure and retinal hemorrhage with papilledema.

cards.front: What four major mechanisms contribute to essential hypertension?
cards.back: Reduced renal sodium excretion, increased vascular resistance, genetic factors, and environmental factors.

cards.front: How does reduced renal sodium excretion raise blood pressure?
cards.back: It increases fluid volume and cardiac output; a higher BP is then needed to excrete sodium.

cards.front: How can chronic vasoconstriction sustain hypertension?
cards.back: It causes permanent arterial wall thickening and sustained elevation of systemic vascular resistance.

cards.front: Which environmental factors can amplify hypertension risk?
cards.back: High salt intake, obesity, physical inactivity, stress, smoking, excess alcohol, and limited healthcare access.

cards.front: What are the three major vascular effects of hypertension?
cards.back: Arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis, and aortic dissection.

cards.front: What are the two histologic forms of arteriolosclerosis in hypertension?
cards.back: Hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.

cards.front: Describe hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
cards.back: Homogeneous pink hyaline thickening of arteriolar walls with loss of structural detail and luminal narrowing.

cards.front: What causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis according to the lecture?
cards.back: Plasma leakage across injured endothelium plus increased ECM production by smooth muscle cells from chronic hemodynamic stress.

cards.front: Describe hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.
cards.back: Onion-skin concentric laminated arteriolar wall thickening with luminal narrowing; laminations contain SMCs and reduplicated basement membrane.

cards.front: What is the main cardiac structural effect of chronic hypertension?
cards.back: Left ventricular wall hypertrophy from increased workload, which can progress to heart failure.

cards.front: How can hypertension cause renal failure?
cards.back: Hyaline or hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis can produce benign or malignant nephrosclerosis and renal failure.

cards.front: What retinal finding is especially associated with malignant hypertension?
cards.back: Retinal hemorrhage and exudate with papilledema.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Cardiac Cycle
decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

cards.front: What is the cardiac cycle?
cards.back: The combined mechanical, electrical, and valvular events occurring during one heartbeat.

cards.front: What opens the AV valves after isovolumetric relaxation?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, creating an atrioventricular pressure gradient.

cards.front: How does ventricular volume change during filling?
cards.back: It rises from ESV toward EDV.

cards.front: What happens to aortic pressure during ventricular filling?
cards.back: It decreases as blood continues to leave the aorta toward the periphery while the aortic valve is closed.

cards.front: What causes S3 in this lecture?
cards.back: Ventricular wall vibration during rapid inflow of blood from atria to ventricles.

cards.front: What is atrial systole's contribution to ventricular filling?
cards.back: About 20–25%; it completes ventricular filling.

cards.front: What causes S4?
cards.back: Ventricular wall vibration during atrial contraction; it is associated with a stiff ventricle.

cards.front: What defines isovolumetric contraction?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure rises while volume remains constant because all valves are closed.

cards.front: What ends isovolumetric contraction?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic/pulmonary pressure and the semilunar valves open.

cards.front: How does ventricular volume change during ejection?
cards.back: It decreases as blood is ejected into the aorta and pulmonary artery.

cards.front: What happens to aortic pressure during ejection?
cards.back: It rises with ventricular pressure during rapid ejection, then begins to fall during reduced ejection.

cards.front: What defines isovolumetric relaxation?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure falls while volume remains constant because all valves are closed.

cards.front: What causes S1?
cards.back: Closure of the AV valves, with vibrations in the ventricles and major vessels.

cards.front: What causes S2?
cards.back: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves.

cards.front: Define EDV.
cards.back: Ventricular blood volume at the end of ventricular diastole.

cards.front: Define ESV.
cards.back: Ventricular blood volume at the end of ventricular systole.

cards.front: How is stroke volume calculated?
cards.back: SV = EDV − ESV.

cards.front: How is ejection fraction calculated?
cards.back: EF = (SV / EDV) × 100.

decks.subject: Pathology
decks.title: Valvular Heart Diseases
decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

cards.front: What is the difference between valvular stenosis and regurgitation?
cards.back: Stenosis = failure to open causing obstruction of forward flow; regurgitation = failure to close causing backflow.

cards.front: What is the most common congenital valvular abnormality listed?
cards.back: Bicuspid aortic valve.

cards.front: What are the major acquired categories of valvular disease?
cards.back: Inflammatory (especially rheumatic/endocarditis) and degenerative (calcific or myxomatous).

cards.front: What are the major causes of aortic stenosis in this lecture?
cards.back: Congenital bicuspid valve, age-related dystrophic calcification, and chronic rheumatic valve disease.

cards.front: What murmur pattern is described for aortic stenosis?
cards.back: Systolic ejection click followed by a crescendo-decrescendo murmur.

cards.front: What major complications follow aortic stenosis?
cards.back: Concentric LV hypertrophy progressing to heart failure, plus angina and syncope.

cards.front: What is the structural defect in mitral valve prolapse?
cards.back: Enlarged, floppy mitral leaflets prolapse into the left atrium because of myxoid degeneration.

cards.front: Which connective-tissue disorders are associated with MVP?
cards.back: Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

cards.front: What causes rheumatic fever?
cards.back: An immune-mediated type II hypersensitivity response after group A β-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis.

cards.front: How does molecular mimicry cause rheumatic fever?
cards.back: Antibodies to streptococcal M protein cross-react with self antigens in myocardium, valves, joints, and other tissues.

cards.front: What does acute rheumatic pancarditis involve?
cards.back: Endocarditis with small vegetations, myocarditis with Aschoff bodies, and fibrinous pericarditis.

cards.front: What is an Aschoff body?
cards.back: A pathognomonic rheumatic granuloma containing T cells, plasma cells, Anitschkow cells, and fibrinoid necrosis.

cards.front: What is an Anitschkow cell?
cards.back: An activated macrophage with abundant cytoplasm and a rod-like nucleus with centrally condensed wavy chromatin.

cards.front: When do acute rheumatic fever manifestations typically appear?
cards.back: About 2–3 weeks after streptococcal infection.

cards.front: What is required for the Jones-criteria diagnosis described in the lecture?
cards.back: Two major criteria, or one major plus two minor criteria, plus evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection.

cards.front: What is the classic valve appearance in chronic rheumatic heart disease?
cards.back: Scarred stenotic mitral valve with a fish-mouth/buttonhole appearance.

cards.front: Which valve is always involved in chronic RHD according to the lecture?
cards.back: The mitral valve; the aortic valve may also be involved.

cards.front: What are important complications of chronic rheumatic valvular disease?
cards.back: Murmurs, chamber hypertrophy/dilatation, heart failure, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, and infective endocarditis.

decks.subject: Physiology
decks.title: Physiology of Vascular Endothelium

cards.front: Name three major ways healthy endothelium keeps blood flowing freely.
cards.back: Antiplatelet + anticoagulant + fibrinolytic actions.

cards.front: What does endothelial thrombomodulin do?
cards.back: Binds thrombin and promotes activation of protein C, supporting anticoagulation.

cards.front: What is the role of protein S in endothelial anticoagulant activity?
cards.back: It acts as a cofactor for activated protein C.

cards.front: What is the effect of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1)?
cards.back: It inhibits fibrinolysis and therefore favors a prothrombotic state.

cards.front: What does von Willebrand factor released by unhealthy/injured endothelium promote?
cards.back: Platelet adhesion.

cards.front: What happens when subendothelial collagen is exposed after endothelial injury?
cards.back: Platelet adhesion and aggregation increase.

cards.front: Which two major endothelial mediators cause vasodilatation?
cards.back: Nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (PGI2).

cards.front: Which major endothelial mediator causes vasoconstriction?
cards.back: Endothelin-1 (ET-1).

cards.front: What is the main angiogenic factor highlighted in the lecture?
cards.back: VEGF - vascular endothelial growth factor.

cards.front: Which two factors inhibit angiogenesis in the lecture?
cards.back: Thrombospondin-1 and endostatin.

cards.front: What metabolic reaction does endothelial ACE perform?
cards.back: Converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, especially in pulmonary endothelium.

cards.front: Which circulating mediators can endothelial cells degrade/inactivate?
cards.back: Bradykinin, serotonin, norepinephrine and prostaglandins.

cards.front: How does healthy endothelium affect local blood flow?
cards.back: It releases vasodilators such as NO and PGI2, increasing blood flow.

cards.front: How does unhealthy endothelium affect local blood flow?
cards.back: It releases vasoconstrictors such as endothelin-1, decreasing blood flow.

cards.front: Which endothelial adhesion molecules regulate leukocyte recruitment?
cards.back: ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and selectins.

cards.front: How does endothelium maintain vascular permeability?
cards.back: Through tight junctions and adherens junctions that regulate movement between endothelial cells.

cards.front: Name major causes of endothelial dysfunction from the lecture.
cards.back: Diabetes/high glucose, high cholesterol/atherosclerosis, hypertension, oxidative stress, metabolic syndrome, septic shock and some autoimmune diseases.

cards.front: What are the major consequences of endothelial dysfunction?
cards.back: Impaired vasomotor tone, thrombosis, inflammation and arterial-wall proliferation -> atherosclerosis and ischemic cardiovascular events.
